solution:
**Correct order of the food chain: Paddy field → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle.**

Three of the four links are stated by the chapter itself. Its paddy-field passage (printed p37) says that “Paddy is cultivated on large scale in various states of South India. Paddy fields are frequently attacked by grasshoppers. Similarly, frogs are also present in large number in the mud of paddy fields, to feed upon grasshoppers and snakes are also present therein to feed upon their favourite food- frogs.” That fixes paddy → grasshopper → frog → snake. The eagle is placed last as the predator of the snake; the chapter does not state the snake–eagle link in its prose, but with the other four members fixed this is the only position left for it.

Trophic roles along the chain:

| Member | Role in the chain |
|---|---|
| Paddy field (the paddy plant) | Producer — the chapter's opening review says “Producers like plants are important” (p36), and its ecosystem chart puts Producer under the autotrophic branch (p37) |
| Grasshopper | Herbivore feeding on the producer |
| Frog | Consumer feeding on the grasshopper |
| Snake | Consumer feeding on the frog |
| Eagle | Last consumer of the chain — the chapter's chart marks a “Tertiary consumer” level (p37) |

**The ecosystem it belongs to.** A paddy field is a cultivated crop field, so this is a **terrestrial, cultivated (man-made) ecosystem** — the chapter states that “Ecosystems are also of two types are natural and artificial” (p42), and a paddy field is grown by human beings. It is an ecosystem in the chapter's own sense because “biotic and abiotic factors occupying a definite geographical area and their interactions collectively constitute the ecosystem” (p38): its biotic factors are the paddy, grasshoppers, frogs, snakes and eagles (together with the decomposers the chapter insists on), and its abiotic factors are the soil, water, air, sunlight and minerals listed in its ecosystem chart (p37).

The chapter also uses this very ecosystem to show ecological balance: it asks what happens “if frog population declines all of a sudden” (p37). With fewer frogs the grasshoppers are eaten less, so their number rises and the paddy crop is damaged more; the snakes lose their favourite food and their number falls, and the eagles above them are affected in turn — so the balance of the whole ecosystem is disturbed by the loss of one link.

An **ancestral property** is something inherited outright from those who came before: the owner may use it, spend it or exhaust it as he pleases, and answers to nobody. Something taken **on lease** is not the holder's at all — it belongs to somebody else, it is only in his keeping for a period, and it must be handed back in good condition. The statement says that the Earth is ours in the second sense and not the first, and that the real owners are the generations still to come.

The chapter prints the statement in exactly this sense (p38): “Human existence is totally impossible without the existence of nature. Hence, it is basic responsibility of human being to preserve the nature without disturbing its balance. It is said that we have got this Earth planet on lease from our future generations and not as an ancestral property from our ancestors. Hence we should not forget to conserve it for ourselves and for future generations.”

What follows from reading it this way:

- We have a **right of use, not a right of destruction**. Natural resources may be used but not exhausted, because they are to be returned.
- The duty is **towards people who cannot yet speak for themselves**. Future generations have no voice in what we do today, which is why the responsibility has to be accepted voluntarily.
- **Conservation is not charity but rent.** Keeping the environment in balance is the condition on which we hold the planet at all.

The chapter makes the same point twice more. It quotes Mahatma Gandhi — “The Earth is sufficient to satisfy everyone's need but not the greed” (p38) — which distinguishes legitimate use from consumption without limit. And it records what happens when the statement is forgotten (p41): “In an attempt to live a satisfactory life, human kept on snatching from the nature as much as possible and this led to increase in problems.”

**Environmental conservation** means protecting the environment from harm and keeping its various factors in balance, so that the living organisms that depend on it can continue to exist.

**Why it is needed.** The chapter explains that “when some natural factors of environment and some artificial polluted factors harm the environment, it creates imbalance between various factors of the environment and ultimately affects the existence of biotic factors” (p38). Pollution of every kind — air, water, sound, soil, thermal and light — has its “Ultimate adverse effect … on existence of all the living organisms and out of this, environmental conservation has become the need of hour” (p39). The chapter's own chart gives the need under two heads (p40): **to solve the natural and artificial problems**, and **to maintain the balance in nature**.

**How it is to be done.** The chapter argues that this cannot be left to rules alone (p40): “General public is not aware about the rules of environment conservation. There should be large scale participation of the people in environment conservation. It will be possible to answer the environmental problems only if environmental protection-conservation becomes an effective public movement.” For that, values “like positive attitude and affection towards environment, knowledge about it, etc. should be inculcated among the children since their childhood”, and awareness is to be increased **through education**.

**What has been done.** “Today, all the developed, developing and underdeveloped countries have accepted the responsibility of environmental protection”, have defined future plans and “have constituted the necessary laws” (p40). The chapter records that the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) was established in 1972 at a conference arranged on human and environment; that a separate environmental department was afterwards established in India; and that the Ministry of environment and forests has been “involved in planning, inducting and increasing awareness about environment and forest through various programs since 1985” (p40).

Finally the chapter makes it a personal duty: human being has “crucial role in maintaining the environmental balance”, and “if human has disturbed the environmental balance, then human itself only can conserve and improve the quality of nature” (p41).

**This chapter does not describe the Chipko Movement, and it does not mention the Bishnoi anywhere at all**, so a short note on it cannot be written from this lesson.

What the chapter actually prints about Chipko is only two things:

- a **“Let’s Discuss” activity box** on printed p41, which says: “Collect the information about Chipko Movement and discuss between two groups of your class about its importance in present situation.” The book is deliberately setting this as outside reading rather than teaching it.
- one entry, **“Chipko Centre, Tehri Garhwal”**, in its list of Voluntary Organizations working for the environment (p43).

The word “Bishnoi” occurs nowhere in the chapter except inside this exercise question itself. So the movement's own history, its people, its dates and its places have to be **collected from outside the textbook, exactly as the book instructs** — they are not in this chapter and should not be written as though they were.

What the chapter **does** supply is the frame into which such a movement fits, and that much can be written from it:

- Conservation succeeds only as a people's effort: “There should be large scale participation of the people in environment conservation. It will be possible to answer the environmental problems only if environmental protection-conservation becomes an effective public movement” (p40).
- Ordinary citizens, not only governments, carry this work: the chapter notes that “Many people in the society are voluntarily coming together to perform this noble work” and lists the voluntary bodies doing it (p43).
- One determined person is enough to begin. The chapter's own example is Jadav Molai Payeng, and it ends: “Many people come together to destroy the forest, but a single person, if determined, can establish a new forest!” (p42).
- Trees are the thing being defended: “Destroying a plant is to destroy everything” and “Forest is Wealth” (p45).

**Biodiversity is the richness of living organisms in nature due to presence of varieties of organisms, ecosystems and genetic variations within a species** (p42). The chapter states that biodiversity occurs at **three different levels**:

| Level | What it is (chapter's own words) | Example the chapter gives |
|---|---|---|
| **Genetic diversity** | “Occurrence of diversity among the organisms of same species is genetic diversity.” | “Each human being is different from other.” |
| **Species diversity** | “Innumerable species of organisms occur in the nature.” It “includes various types of plants, animals and microbes.” | — (the chapter gives no named example here) |
| **Ecosystem diversity** | “Many ecosystems are present in each region.” Each “has its own characteristic animals, plants, microbes and abiotic factors.” | Ecosystems “are also of two types are natural and artificial.” |

**Why it matters.** The chapter warns under genetic diversity that “Possibility of wiping out the species arises if there is decrease in the diversity within the species whose members involve in sexual reproduction” (p42). It also observes that “Our living world had been richly diverse”, yet “we are not able to see some specific animals about which we had listened from our earlier generations”, and that the “Most harmful effect of the environmental pollution occurs on the living organisms” (p42).

The chapter notes that **22nd May is World Biodiversity Day** (p45).

**“The forest conserved in the name of god and considered to be sacred is called as sacred grove”** (p43).

The chapter's points about them:

- They are **in fact ‘sanctuaries’**, but ones “conserved by the society and not by the government forest department” — so the protection is social, not official.
- “As it has been conserved in the name of god, it has **special protection**.” Religious sentiment does the work that a law would otherwise have to do.
- They are **clusters of thick forest**, “present not only in Western Ghats of India but in the entire country”.
- **“More than 13000 sacred groves have been reported in India.”**

The chapter then sets the reader a task on them: “Where are such sacred groves in Maharashtra? Make a list and visit with your teachers.” It does not itself name any individual sacred grove.

Sacred groves matter for this lesson because they are a working example of the chapter's central claim that conservation succeeds when it becomes a people's practice rather than only a rule — and of its list of ways to conserve biodiversity, which includes “Maintaining record of traditional knowledge” (p43).

**This chapter does not deal with disasters or their management.** The word “disaster” appears nowhere in the lesson except inside this exercise question — checked against the whole chapter (printed pp 36–46).

**Disaster and its management is the subject of a separate chapter of this same book**: Science and Technology Part II, chapter 10, “Disaster Management” (printed pp 109–120). The short note should be written from there, not from this lesson.

The only material in this chapter that comes near the idea is its box on **radioactive pollution** (p40), which records that “Chernobyl, Windscale, and Three Miles Island mishaps are the major mishaps of the world till present” and that “Thousands of people have been affected for long term due to these accidents”. The effects it lists are:

1. “Cancerous ulceration occurs due to higher radiations of X-rays.”
2. “Tissues in the body are destroyed.”
3. “Genetic changes occur.”
4. “Vision is adversely affected.”

That is a record of man-made accidents and their long-term harm, and it shows why prevention matters — but the chapter offers no definition of a disaster, no classification of disasters, and no account of how one is managed.

Overcoming pollution is a powerful way of environmental management because, on this chapter's own account, pollution is **the main cause of the environmental problems that management exists to solve**, and it is a cause that lies within human control. The justification can be built in five steps, all from the chapter.

**1. Pollution is named as the chief problem.** “At present, many environmental problems have been arisen due to effect of various natural and artificial factors on the Earth. **Environmental pollution is one of those main factors**” (p39).

**2. It attacks every part of the environment at once.** Pollution is “direct or indirect changes in physical, chemical and biological properties of air, water and soil which will be harmful to humans and other living beings” (p39). The chapter lists air, water, sound, soil, thermal and light pollution, and says the “Ultimate adverse effect of all these is on existence of all the living organisms and out of this, environmental conservation has become the need of hour” (p39). Removing pollution therefore protects air, water and soil together, rather than one at a time.

**3. Its worst harm falls on life itself, and some of it cannot be undone.** “Most harmful effect of the environmental pollution occurs on the living organisms” (p42) — it is why species that earlier generations knew are no longer seen. Radioactive pollution shows how permanent the damage can be: thousands affected for the long term by the Chernobyl, Windscale and Three Miles Island mishaps, with cancerous ulceration, destruction of tissues, genetic changes and damage to vision (p40). Prevention is therefore worth far more than any later remedy.

**4. Its causes are human, so they can be managed.** The chapter's list of reasons is entirely a list of human choices — “population explosion, fast industrialization, and indiscriminate use of natural resources, deforestation, and unplanned urbanization” (p39). What people cause, people can control; and the chapter insists that “if human has disturbed the environmental balance, then human itself only can conserve and improve the quality of nature” (p41).

**5. The country's environmental management already works mainly through pollution control.** The purpose of the Environmental (Protection) Act, 1986 “is to control the pollution and punish the persons or institutes harming the environment”, and under it “Any person or factory is prohibited … from releasing the pollutants in atmosphere beyond a permissible limit”, with the National Green Tribunal established in 2010 for effective implementation (p41). The other rules the chapter lists are pollution-control instruments too — the Sound Pollution (Control & Prevention) Rule, 2000, the Biomedical Waste (Management & Handling) Rule, 1998, and the E-waste (Management & Handling) Rule, 2011 (p41).

**Conclusion.** Controlling pollution removes the principal cause of imbalance between the factors of the environment, protects the existence of all living organisms and of biodiversity, prevents damage that cannot later be repaired, and acts on causes that are within human power — which is why it is a powerful, and not merely one, way of managing the environment. As the chapter puts it in its closing list, “Pure air, pure water is key to healthy life” (p45).

This question asks for the student's **own** plan, and the chapter supplies a menu to choose from rather than one correct answer. It says directly: “You can be a conservator, organizer, guide, plant-friend, etc. Describe about the role you wish to perform and your plans for that role” (p42), and prints a **“My Role in Environment”** chart (p44) with six roles — Conservation, Preservation, Prevention, Control, Production and Awareness.

Projects that follow directly from the chapter, and how each would be run:

| Project | How it would be run, from the chapter |
|---|---|
| **Tree plantation / afforestation drive** | The chapter's instruction is “Practice afforestation to conserve environment” and “Destroying a plant is to destroy everything” (p45). Its model is Jadav Molai Payeng, who planted and cared for trees until a barren area carried forest over 1360 acres (p42). Plant, and then keep caring for what is planted. |
| **Biodiversity register of my locality** | “Survey the plants and animals in your area. Maintain a record about their characteristics” (p45); the chapter also lists “Maintaining record of traditional knowledge” as a way of conserving biodiversity (p43). |
| **Sacred-grove listing and visit** | “Where are such sacred groves in Maharashtra? Make a list and visit with your teachers” (p43). |
| **Paper-saving drive in school** | “Provident use of paper is prevention of deforestation” (p45). |
| **Pollution-control project** | Pollution is the main cause of environmental problems (p39); a project can target one kind — sound, biomedical waste or e-waste — along the lines of the rules the chapter lists for each (p41). |
| **Protection of a rare local species** | “Protecting the rare species of organisms” and “Projects for conservation of special species” are two of the chapter's seven ways to conserve biodiversity (p43). |
| **Awareness campaign** | The Awareness box of the role chart gives the method: education, guidance, awareness, imitation, organization, participation (p44). The chapter argues conservation works “only if environmental protection-conservation becomes an effective public movement” with “large scale participation of the people” (p40). |

**How to run any of them, in the chapter's own order of work.** Pick a role from the chart and plan under its four headings: **Prevention** — prevent possible harms and design new plans; **Control** — prevent the harm, stop the harmful activities and change the mindset; **Preservation** — preserve whatever has been left over and prevent further loss; **Production** — revive the harmed factors of the environment and attempt innovation (p44). Work with others rather than alone, since the chapter's whole argument is that this must become a public movement (p40), and help can be sought from the bodies it lists, such as the Bombay Natural History Society, the Centre for Environment Education or the Chipko Centre (p43). Finally, follow the rules — “Observing the rules” is itself one of the seven conservation measures (p43).

The chapter divides the factors affecting the environment into **natural factors** and **manmade factors** (flow chart, p38):

| Class of factor | What the chapter puts under it |
|---|---|
| **Natural factors** | **Earthquakes** — the one example the book itself prints. To it belong the natural components it names elsewhere: air, atmosphere, water, land and living organisms (p38), and the abiotic factors of its ecosystem chart — air, water, vapour, minerals, soil and sunlight, and the inorganic substances hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, calcium, iron, sodium and potassium (p37). |
| **Manmade factors** | **Deforestation** — the one example the book itself prints. To it belong the human causes it names for environmental pollution: population explosion, fast industrialization, indiscriminate use of natural resources, deforestation and unplanned urbanization (p39). |

More basically, the chapter says that **“environment consists of two basic factors- 1. Biotic factors, 2. Abiotic factors”** (p38), and defines the environment itself as “Physical, chemical and biological factors affecting the living organisms in any possible way” (p37). It adds that there are two main types of environment, natural and artificial, and that “Artificial environment is also affecting the natural environment directly or indirectly” (p37–38).

The chapter also names the things that keep these factors in balance: “various natural cycles like water cycle, carbon cycle, gaseous cycles like nitrogen cycle, oxygen cycle, etc.”, and “various food chains of ecosystem” (p38).

Note that the book prints this flow chart as an **“Observe and fill the information” activity** with only one example filled in under each head; the remaining entries above are gathered from the chapter's own prose.

Human beings have an important place in the environment because, of all the organisms in it, **only they can deliberately change the balance of nature — and therefore only they can repair it.** The chapter puts it directly (p41): “human has crucial role in maintaining the environmental balance. **If human has disturbed the environmental balance, then human itself only can conserve and improve the quality of nature.**”

The chapter's reasoning, in its own order:

- **Humans arrived last but rose above the rest.** “Human stepped on the Earth long after formation of Earth. On the Earth, human being proved its superiority as compared to other animals with the help of characters like **intelligence, memory, imaginary ability**, etc.” (p41)
- **They came to dominate nature.** “Human established domination over the nature. Human utilized all the natural resources as much as possible.” (p41)
- **That domination has been the source of the damage.** “In an attempt to live a satisfactory life, human kept on snatching from the nature as much as possible and this led to increase in problems.” (p41) The causes of pollution the chapter lists — population explosion, fast industrialization, indiscriminate use of natural resources, deforestation, unplanned urbanization (p39) — are all human doing.
- **Yet humans cannot survive apart from nature.** “Human existence is totally impossible without the existence of nature. Hence, it is basic responsibility of human being to preserve the nature without disturbing its balance.” (p38)
- **Hence the responsibility is theirs alone.** The chapter adds a warning that this responsibility is often not even noticed: “Many times, general public is unknown that its activities are harmful to environment and thereby unknowingly many activities happen” (p41) — which is why it calls for awareness through education (p40).

So the human place in the environment is important in two opposite ways at once: humans are the greatest single disturber of the environmental balance, and they are the only agent capable of consciously restoring it.

The chapter states that **“Biodiversity occurs at three different levels”** (p42):

| Type | Definition given in the chapter | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Genetic diversity** | “Occurrence of diversity among the organisms of same species is genetic diversity.” | “Each human being is different from other” — the chapter's own example. |
| **Species diversity** | “Innumerable species of organisms occur in the nature. This is called as species diversity.” It “includes various types of plants, animals and microbes.” | The chapter gives no named example under this head; the three groups it names — plants, animals and microbes — are what species diversity covers. |
| **Ecosystem diversity** | “Many ecosystems are present in each region. Ecosystem is formed through the interaction between plants, animals, their habitat and changes in the environment. Each ecosystem has its own characteristic animals, plants, microbes and abiotic factors.” | “Ecosystems are also of two types are natural and artificial” — the chapter's own division. Elsewhere it names a small pond as an ecosystem and the Earth as the largest ecosystem (p38). |

The chapter also notes the consequence of losing genetic diversity: “Possibility of wiping out the species arises if there is decrease in the diversity within the species whose members involve in sexual reproduction” (p42).

The chapter answers this question directly, in a box headed **“How can biodiversity be conserved?”** (p43). Its seven measures are:

1. Protecting the rare species of organisms.
2. Establishing national parks and sanctuaries.
3. Declaring some regions as ‘bioreserves’.
4. Projects for conservation of special species.
5. Conserving all plants and animals.
6. Observing the rules.
7. Maintaining record of traditional knowledge.

The chapter supports several of these elsewhere:

- **Observing the rules** is backed by the laws it lists (p41): the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, which prohibits land reserved for forest conservation from being used for any other purpose; the Environmental (Protection) Act, 1986, whose purpose “is to control the pollution and punish the persons or institutes harming the environment”, with the National Green Tribunal established in 2010 for its effective implementation; and the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, under whose clause 49 A “trading of rare animals has been completely banned”, clause 49 B bans “use of articles prepared from skin or organs of wild animals”, and clause 49 C makes “disclosure of the stock of artefacts made form rare wild animals” compulsory.
- **Society's own sanctuaries** already do this work: sacred groves are “in fact ‘sanctuaries’ conserved by the society and not by the government forest department”, and more than 13000 of them have been reported in India (p43).
- **Knowing which species are at risk** comes first: the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) “prepares the ‘Red List’ that contains the names of endangered species from different countries”, whose pink pages carry endangered species and green pages those “previously endangered but presently safe” (p45).
- **People must be involved**, because “It will be possible to answer the environmental problems only if environmental protection-conservation becomes an effective public movement” (p40).

The chapter tells the story under the heading **“The big story of a small man”** (p42). Jadav Molai Payeng of Assam, born in 1963, has worked as a forest worker since the age of 16. When a large number of snakes died in a flood of the Brahmaputra River flowing by his village, he planted **20 bamboo plantlets** as a preventive measure. In 1979 the local Social Forestry Department began a social afforestation project on 200 hectares of land and Molai was one of the few forest workers looking after it — **and he continued to plant trees even after the project was completed.** By his continuous planting and caring, over about 30 years the barren area came to carry forest cover over **1360 acres**. This jungle in Kokilamukh of Jorhat district of Assam is now known as **‘Molai Jungle’**, and he has been awarded the **‘Padmashree’** by the government of India for this unparalleled work.

What we learn from it:

- **One determined person is enough.** The chapter draws the lesson itself: “Many people come together to destroy the forest, but a single person, if determined, can establish a new forest!”
- **Persistence matters more than scale of resources.** He began with twenty bamboo plantlets and no authority, and the forest is the result of thirty years of steady work.
- **Do not stop when the duty ends.** The decisive act was continuing to plant after the official project was over — conservation is a personal commitment, not a job that finishes.
- **Concern for other organisms is a good enough reason to act.** He began because snakes had died in a flood.
- **Restoration is possible.** Barren land can be turned back into forest, which supports the chapter's own instruction to “Practice afforestation to conserve environment” (p45).
- **Such work is recognised by society**, as the Padmashree shows.

(A note on the name: the exercise spells it “Peyang”, while the chapter's own story box on p42 spells it “Payeng”. The book is inconsistent; the same person is meant.)

**The chapter does not name a single biodiversity hotspot**, so this list cannot be written from it.

Its section “Hotspots of Biodiversity” (p44) gives only figures:

- **34** highly sensitive biodiversity spots are reported all over the world.
- Such areas had once occupied **15.7%** of the area of the Earth.
- At present **86%** of the sensitive areas are already destroyed, so only **2.3%** of the Earth's area is left with sensitive spots.
- These include **1,50,000 plant species**, which are **50%** of the world count.
- For India: out of **135 species of animals, 85** are found in the jungles of the **eastern region**; about **1,500 endemic plant species** are found in the **western ghat**; and of the total plant species in the entire world, **50,000** are endemic.

The section then ends by telling the student directly: “**Collect more information about locations of these hotspots present in the world.**” The book is asking for a list it has chosen not to print, so the names have to be collected from an atlas or another source.

The only Indian regions this chapter itself singles out as rich and threatened are in its box **“Three Endangered Heritage Places of the Country”** (p44) — and it is worth being clear that **the chapter does not call these three ‘hotspots’**:

| Place | Why it is endangered, per the chapter |
|---|---|
| **The Western Ghat**, spread over Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Tamilnadu and Kerala | Mining industry and search for natural gas; habitats of Asiatic lion and wild bison are under threat |
| **Manas National Park**, Assam | Dams and indiscriminate use of water; tiger and rhino of that region are under threat |
| **Sunderban National Park**, West Bengal | Reserved for tigers, but the tiger population and local environment are challenged by dams, deforestation, excessive fishing and the trenches dug for it |

Of these, the Western Ghat is the one the chapter connects to hotspot data, since it is where it places the 1,500 endemic plant species.

**(The book prints this as a second sub-item lettered “f.”, immediately after the previous “f.”; there is no “g.”.)**

**Why many species of plants and animals are endangered.** The chapter's reasons, gathered from across the lesson:

| Reason | Where the chapter says it |
|---|---|
| **Pollution** — its “Most harmful effect … occurs on the living organisms”, which is why species earlier generations knew are no longer seen | p42 |
| **Destruction and shrinking of habitat** — a species becomes endangered when “their habitat is shrunk to such an extent that they can be extinct in near future” | p45 |
| **Mining and the search for natural gas** — endangering the Western Ghat and the habitats of Asiatic lion and wild bison | p44 |
| **Dams and indiscriminate use of water** — threatening tiger and rhino at Manas National Park | p44 |
| **Deforestation, excessive fishing and trenching** — challenging the tigers of Sunderban National Park | p44 |
| **Trade in wild animals and in articles made from their skin and organs** — the conduct the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 had to ban outright under clauses 49 A and 49 B | p41 |
| **Loss of genetic diversity** — “Possibility of wiping out the species arises if there is decrease in the diversity within the species” | p42 |
| **The general human causes of environmental damage** — population explosion, fast industrialization, indiscriminate use of natural resources, deforestation and unplanned urbanization | p39 |

The chapter shows how fast this is happening: a World Wildlife Fund (WWF) survey published in **2008** found that “about **30%** of animal species have become extinct over the period of **35 years (1975 – 2005)**”, and asks “What will happen in future if this continues as it is?” (p45). It also classifies what is at risk — **endangered species** (lion tailed monkey, lesser florican), **rare species** (red panda, musk deer), **vulnerable species** (tiger, lion) and **indeterminate species** (giant squirrel / shekru) (p45).

**How they can be saved.** The chapter's seven measures (p43):

1. Protecting the rare species of organisms.
2. Establishing national parks and sanctuaries.
3. Declaring some regions as ‘bioreserves’.
4. Projects for conservation of special species.
5. Conserving all plants and animals.
6. Observing the rules.
7. Maintaining record of traditional knowledge.

To these the chapter adds: **enforcing the laws** — the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 and the Environmental (Protection) Act, 1986, with the National Green Tribunal established in 2010 (p41); **controlling pollution**, since it is the main cause of harm to living organisms (p39, p42); **identifying what is at risk**, through the IUCN ‘Red List’ of endangered species (p45); **protection by society itself**, as in the more than 13000 sacred groves of India (p43); and **making conservation a public movement** through awareness and education, since “It will be possible to answer the environmental problems only if environmental protection-conservation becomes an effective public movement” (p40).

**The chapter nowhere prints the meaning of these symbols.** Its own “Enlist and discuss” box on printed p43 shows four **different** symbols and likewise only asks the student to “Find the meaning of those symbols in relation to environment conservation. Make a list of other such symbols.” The words “recycling” and “solar” do not occur anywhere in the lesson. So the meanings below are read off the pictures themselves, and the roles are taken from the chapter's **“My Role in Environment”** chart (p44) and its closing “Always Remember” list (p45).

| Symbol as printed | What it stands for | My role accordingly |
|---|---|---|
| Three green arrows chasing one another in a triangle | **Recycling** — waste material should be sent back into use instead of being thrown away | Separate waste at home and school and give it for recycling instead of discarding it. The chapter's rules on **Biomedical Waste (Management & Handling), 1998** and **E-waste (Management & Handling), 2011** (p41) exist for exactly this, and “Observing the rules” is one of its conservation measures (p43). |
| A water drop closing a tap | **Save water — do not let it run to waste** | Close taps, repair leaks and use water sparingly. The chapter lists water among the abiotic factors every ecosystem depends on (p37) and ends with “Pure air, pure water is key to healthy life” (p45). |
| A green solar panel | **Use energy from the sun instead of polluting sources** | Prefer solar water heating and solar lighting, and use electricity carefully. The chapter names “fast industrialization” and the gases and smoke of air pollution — CO2, CO, hydrocarbons, sulphur, NOx, hydrogen sulphide — among the causes of environmental damage (p39), and records that radiation from atomic energy plants is an artificial radioactive pollutant (p40). |

**Writing my role generally.** The chapter's chart (p44) gives six roles to choose from, and the answer to “write your role accordingly” should be written under them: **Conservation** — conserving the available resources; **Preservation** — preserving whatever has been left over and preventing further loss; **Prevention** — preventing possible harms and designing new plans; **Control** — preventing the harm, stopping harmful activities and changing the mindset; **Production** — reviving harmed factors of the environment; **Awareness** — education, guidance, awareness, imitation, organization and participation. The chapter's own summing-up is the shortest statement of the role: “I will make the change that I am expecting” (Pledge for Life, p46).
